tip: ‘syrthio i gysgu’ is the set phrase for fall asleep, literally fall to sleep: ‘syrthiodd e i gysgu’.
‘byddwn ni’ = we will (future). Swap ‘ni’ for ‘i’ and ‘byddwn i’ means I would (conditional). The pronoun sets the meaning.
‘yn’ plus a verb gives an -ing sense after hearing or seeing verbs: ‘y plant yn chwerthin’ = the children laughing.
The linking word ‘o’ (of) softens the next consonant: ‘plant’ (children) becomes ‘o blant’ here.
‘wedi’ replaces ‘yn’ to make the have-done past: ‘mae hi wedi ysgrifennu’ = she has written.
‘i’ before a verb shows purpose: ‘i adael’ = in order to let. ‘agorodd hi'r ffenest i adael awyr’ = opened it to let air.
The -est ending is -af: ‘hen’ (old) becomes ‘hynaf’ (oldest) in ‘yr ieithoedd hynaf’ (the oldest languages).
Welsh says half past as ‘hanner awr wedi tri’, literally half an hour past three. Here ‘wedi’ means past.
‘roeddwn i fod i’ means I was supposed to; ‘i fod i’ marks an arranged or expected action.
‘fy’ (my) triggers nasal mutation: ‘côt’ becomes ‘nghôt’. So ‘fy nghôt’ means my coat.
‘o’ (of) triggers soft mutation: ‘Mehefin’ becomes ‘Fehefin’. The month softens after ‘o’ in dates.
The object after a past-tense verb softens its first word: ‘dwy’ becomes ‘ddwy’ in ‘prynais i ddwy gôt’.
Welsh past tense keeps verb-then-subject order: ‘derbyniodd e'r cynnig’ = he accepted the offer, verb first.
‘shw' mae’ is the south Wales greeting for how are you. The north says ‘sut mae’ instead.
Welsh puts the verb first: the sentence opens with the verb, then ‘y storm’, then ‘y to’ (the roof).
‘ei’ (his) triggers soft mutation: ‘tad’ becomes ‘dad’. So ‘ei dad’ means his father.
After a number the noun stays singular: ‘pum cannwyll’ is literally five candle, not candles.
‘pump’ (five) shortens to ‘bum’ before a noun, which stays singular: ‘bum milltir’ = five miles, not a plural.
‘bod’ carries that in a fact clause: ‘y ffaith bod e yma’ means the fact that he is here.
‘dwy’ is the feminine two and softens the noun: ‘pont’ becomes ‘bont’. ‘dwy bont’ means two bridges.
‘sy’ is the word for which is or that is: ‘y gardd sy tu ôl’ means the garden that is behind.
Report that with a ‘bod’ form: ‘cwynodd hi fod y gwasanaeth yn wael’ = she complained that the service was poor.
Age uses ‘yn’ plus ‘oed’: ‘naw deg oed’ means ninety years old, literally ninety of age.
‘diolch byth’ is a set phrase for thank goodness, literally thanks ever.
Welsh four changes by gender: ‘pedwar’ with masculine nouns like ‘tymor’, ‘pedair’ with feminine ones.
Negatives usually add ‘ddim’ after the verb: ‘dydyn ni ddim’ means we do not.
‘gyda’ becomes ‘gydag’ before a vowel: ‘gydag un cam’ means with one step.
Welsh has no verb for need: ‘mae angen’ X ‘ar’ Y means Y needs X. Here ‘ar ei gar’ makes it his car needs a battery.
‘wedi’ means past when telling time: ‘chwarter wedi dau’ is quarter past two.
‘wrth eu bodd’ is an idiom for delighted, literally at their pleasure.
